content: Neonates often undergo numerous painful procedures due to diagnostic, therapeutic, or surgical needs. Pain management options for these infants include opioids, non-pharmacological interventions, and other medications. Among opioids, morphine, fentanyl, and remifentanil are the most commonly used in neonates. However, there is evidence suggesting that opioids may negatively affect the developing brain's structure and function. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and harms of using opioids in term or preterm neonates experiencing procedural pain. Comparisons were made between opioids and placebo or no drug, non-pharmacological interventions, other analgesics or sedatives, other opioids, or the same opioid administered via different routes. The review included randomized controlled trials involving preterm and term neonates up to a postmenstrual age of 46 weeks. Thirteen studies, enrolling a total of 823 neonates, were included. Seven studies compared opioids to placebo or no treatment, two studies compared opioids to oral sweet solutions or non-pharmacological interventions, and five studies compared opioids to other analgesics or sedatives. All studies were conducted in hospital settings. When opioids were compared to placebo or no drug, the following findings were observed: Opioids likely reduce pain scores during procedures as measured by the Premature Infant Pain Profile (PIPP) or PIPP-Revised (PIPP-R) scale (moderate-certainty evidence). Opioids may reduce pain scores during procedures as measured by the Neonatal Infant Pain Scale (NIPS) (low-certainty evidence). Opioids may result in little to no difference in pain scores one to two hours after the procedure, as measured by the Douleur Aiguë du Nouveau-né (DAN) scale (low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of opioids on pain scores assessed with the PIPP/PIPP-R scale up to 30 minutes or one to two hours after the procedure (very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of opioids on episodes of bradycardia (very low-certainty evidence). Opioids may increase episodes of apnea compared to placebo (low-certainty evidence), with one study reporting a concerning increase in severe apnea (very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of opioids on episodes of hypotension (very low-certainty evidence). No studies reported on parent satisfaction with care in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU). When opioids were compared to non-pharmacological interventions: The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of opioids on pain scores during procedures, as measured by the CRIES (Crying, Requires oxygen, Increased vital signs, Expression, Sleep) scale, when compared to facilitated tucking or sensorial stimulation (very low-certainty evidence). Other main outcomes were not reported. When opioids were compared to other analgesics or sedatives: The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of opioids on pain scores during procedures, up to 30 minutes after the procedure, or one to two hours after the procedure, as measured by the PIPP/PIPP-R scale (very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of opioids on episodes of apnea during or after the procedure (very low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of opioids on episodes of hypotension (very low-certainty evidence). Other main outcomes were not reported. No studies were identified that compared different opioids (e.g., morphine versus fentanyl) or different routes of administration for the same opioid (e.g., enteral versus intravenous morphine). In conclusion, compared to placebo, opioids likely reduce pain scores during procedures as measured by the PIPP/PIPP-R scale, may reduce pain scores as measured by the NIPS, and may result in little to no difference in pain scores one to two hours after the procedure as measured by the DAN scale. However, the evidence is very uncertain regarding the effects of opioids on other pain scores, at different time points, or on episodes of bradycardia, hypotension, or severe apnea. Opioids may increase episodes of apnea. No studies reported parent satisfaction with NICU care. The evidence is very uncertain about the effects of opioids compared to non-pharmacological interventions or other analgesics. Additionally, no studies compared different opioids or routes of administration.
